versions.problem: Can MVFA's segmentation adapters be trained without any pixel masks, using only image-level normal/abnormal labels on all six BMAD source datasets, by replacing the Dice + Focal targets with pseudo-masks derived from the frozen CLIP patch features (patches of an abnormal training image that have no close neighbour among the patches of normal images of the same dataset), and how much of the zero-shot pixel-level AUROC and Dice of the mask-supervised MVFA does this recover on a held-out modality?
versions.rationale: MVFA's anomaly maps come only from the segmentation adapters, which are trained with Dice and Focal losses on BrainMRI, LiverCT and RESC masks (G3); the three image-only datasets (OCT17, ChestXray, HIS) never contribute localisation supervision, and the few-shot setting additionally assumes K masked abnormal images (G4). The related work shows that weaker signals can supervise localisation: CoDeGraph [30] filters consistent anomalies with batch-level patch graphs and shows that the resulting pseudo-masks can supervise prompt-driven vision-language models; DDAD [54] exploits unlabelled abnormal images alongside normal ones; MediCLIP [10] and SpatioPrompt [20] adapt CLIP from normal images with synthetic anomalies; MedSAD-CLIP [8] instead assumes real masks. None of these tests whether MVFA's multi-level residual adapters, the target method's own component, can be trained from image-level labels alone. The question is fine-grained (one loss target of one branch), feasible on BMAD with one GPU because pseudo-masks are computed once with frozen features, and measurable under the shared protocol: pixel AUROC and Dice on BrainMRI, LiverCT and RESC when held out, compared with the re-run mask-supervised MVFA, plus the effect of adding the three mask-free datasets as localisation sources. A positive answer removes MVFA's dependence on dense expert masks; a negative one quantifies how much masks are worth.

Clarity.review: The component (segmentation-adapter targets), the supervision (image-level labels on six sources), the pseudo-mask rule and the outcome (fraction of mask-supervised pixel AUROC and Dice recovered) are all named. The pseudo-mask rule leaves its threshold ('no close neighbour') and the feature level it is computed on undefined.
Clarity.feedback: State the pseudo-mask rule operationally: which CLIP level, which distance, and how the threshold is chosen without target labels (for example a percentile of normal-to-normal distances on source validation data).

Relevance.review: Directly addresses G3, the dependence of localisation on dense masks from three datasets, and uses the three image-only BMAD sources that MVFA currently cannot use for localisation. It builds on CoDeGraph's pseudo-mask supervision and the weak-supervision line in the review set.
Relevance.feedback: Make the link to G4 explicit only if the same mechanism is also tested in the few-shot setting; otherwise keep the focus on zero-shot source training.

Originality.review: Pseudo-masks from patch-level nearest-neighbour discrepancy are known (PatchCore-style scoring, CoDeGraph uses batch-level graphs to supervise prompt-driven VLMs), and weakly supervised localisation is a mature area. The new element is the question of whether MVFA's multi-level adapters can be trained this way and what the image-only datasets contribute; that is a useful but moderate step.
Originality.feedback: Sharpen what is new relative to CoDeGraph: for example, that the pseudo-masks come from labelled abnormal images rather than unlabeled batches, so image-level labels can veto false positives.

Feasibility.review: Pseudo-masks are computed once with frozen features and then replace the mask loader; training cost equals MVFA's. The risk is pseudo-mask quality on low-contrast modalities (ChestXray, HIS), which could make the comparison uninformative.
Feasibility.feedback: Plan a pseudo-mask quality check on the three masked datasets (pseudo vs true mask IoU) before training, so a negative result can be attributed.

Significance.review: Removing the need for dense masks would let MVFA use any image-level labelled archive and would show how much expert annotation actually buys; either outcome is informative for clinical adoption.
Significance.feedback: Report results as a label-cost curve (no masks, masks on one dataset, masks on three) to make the significance concrete.

versions.problem: Can MVFA's segmentation adapters be trained without pixel masks, using pseudo-masks from labelled abnormal source images only (a patch of an abnormal image is marked anomalous when its frozen CLIP level-4 feature lies farther from every patch of the same dataset's normal images than the 99th percentile of normal-to-normal nearest-neighbour distances on source validation data), and how much of the zero-shot pixel AUROC and Dice of the mask-supervised MVFA does this recover on a held-out modality, as masks are removed from zero, one, or all three masked source datasets?
versions.rationale: MVFA's anomaly maps come only from the segmentation adapters, which are trained with Dice and Focal losses on masks of BrainMRI, LiverCT and RESC (G3); the three image-only datasets (OCT17, ChestXray, HIS) never supervise localisation. The question is what dense expert masks actually buy. Unlike CoDeGraph [30], which derives pseudo-masks from unlabelled batches and must first filter consistent anomalies, here image-level labels veto false positives: pseudo-masks are drawn only from images known to be abnormal and are defined against normal images of the same dataset, with a threshold fixed on source data. DDAD [54], MediCLIP [10] and SpatioPrompt [20] use unlabelled or synthetic signals in other frameworks; none tests MVFA's own multi-level adapters. The answer is reported as a label-cost curve (masks on three, one or zero sources, plus the three image-only datasets added as pseudo-mask sources), and pseudo-mask quality is first measured against true masks on the three masked datasets (IoU, pixel AUROC) so that a negative result can be attributed. One loss target of one branch changes; pseudo-masks are computed once with frozen features, so the cost equals MVFA's training under the shared leave-one-modality-out protocol.

Clarity.review: The pseudo-mask rule is now operational (feature level, distance, threshold fixed on source validation data), and the outcome is a precise label-cost curve.
Clarity.feedback: Keep the threshold percentile as a reported hyper-parameter with a small sensitivity check.

Relevance.review: Directly addresses G3 and makes use of the three image-only BMAD sources; the zero-shot focus is now explicit.

Originality.review: Using image-level labels to restrict pseudo-masks to known abnormal images is a sensible distinction from CoDeGraph's unlabelled batches, but nearest-neighbour pseudo-masks and weakly supervised localisation remain established ideas; the main novelty is the question asked of MVFA.
Originality.feedback: The originality would rise if the pseudo-masks were refined by MVFA itself during training (self-training) rather than fixed, but that would widen the problem.

Feasibility.review: Computationally cheap and well planned, with an upfront pseudo-mask quality check. Pseudo-mask quality on ChestXray and HIS remains a risk for the image-only extension.
Feasibility.feedback: Treat the image-only extension as secondary so the main result does not depend on it.

Significance.review: A label-cost curve would directly tell practitioners how much expert annotation MVFA needs; useful for the field regardless of outcome.

versions.problem: How much of the zero-shot localisation quality of MVFA (pixel AUROC and Dice on a held-out modality) is retained when its segmentation adapters are trained without pixel masks, using pseudo-masks drawn only from labelled abnormal source images (a patch is anomalous when its frozen CLIP level-4 feature is farther from every normal patch of the same dataset than the 99th percentile of normal-to-normal nearest-neighbour distances on source validation data), as masks are removed from zero, one, or all three masked source datasets?
versions.rationale: MVFA's anomaly maps come only from segmentation adapters trained with Dice and Focal losses on masks of BrainMRI, LiverCT and RESC (G3), so the method cannot learn localisation from image-level labelled archives, and the value of dense expert masks is unknown. Unlike CoDeGraph [30], which builds pseudo-masks from unlabelled batches and must filter consistent anomalies, image-level labels here restrict pseudo-masks to images known to be abnormal and define them against normal images of the same dataset, with a threshold fixed on source data only (its percentile is reported with a small sensitivity check). DDAD [54], MediCLIP [10] and SpatioPrompt [20] use unlabelled or synthetic signals in other frameworks; none tests MVFA's multi-level adapters. The primary result is a label-cost curve on the three masked datasets, preceded by a pseudo-mask quality check against true masks so that a negative result can be attributed; adding the image-only datasets (OCT17, ChestXray, HIS) as pseudo-mask sources is a secondary analysis. One loss target of one branch changes, pseudo-masks are computed once, and training cost equals MVFA's under the shared protocol.

Clarity.review: One question with an operational pseudo-mask rule, a threshold fixed on source data, and a precisely defined primary outcome (label-cost curve) with a secondary analysis clearly separated.

Relevance.review: Directly addresses G3, the dependence of MVFA's localisation on dense masks.

Originality.review: The label-restricted pseudo-mask construction is a reasonable twist on known nearest-neighbour pseudo-labelling; the question asked of MVFA is new but the mechanism is not.

Feasibility.review: Pseudo-masks computed once; training cost equals MVFA's; the risky image-only extension is now secondary, and the quality check makes negative results interpretable.

Significance.review: Tells practitioners how much expert annotation MVFA needs and whether image-level archives suffice.

versions.problem: Can the transductive test-set min-max normalisation, fixed 0.5 fusion weight and max-over-pixels image score of MVFA's few-shot inference be replaced by a per-image score computed only from the K-shot support images and source-modality validation data, such that image-level AUROC stays within 1 point of the re-run baseline while the scores become threshold-ready (sensitivity at 95% specificity, expected calibration error) and invariant to the composition of the test set (prevalence and outlier resampling)?
versions.rationale: The released code normalises each branch with the minimum and maximum over the entire test set before fusing them with weight 0.5 (G8), and the image AUC on masked datasets is the maximum of the fused map, so one spurious pixel decides the label (G9); only threshold-free AUC is reported (G11). A deployed system scores one image at a time, so the published numbers are not those of a usable detector. Recent CLIP detectors in the review set treat scoring and fusion as a design problem of its own: LaRP-CLIP [17] criticises fixed fusion strategies and global-similarity image scores, HeadCLIP [4] proposes a joint anomaly score that uses pixel-level information, and CANOR [55] shows that a handful of calibration scalars and a principled aggregation rule improve CLIP scores without retraining the encoder. None addresses the transductive normalisation that MVFA's results depend on. The problem concerns one component (the inference-time scoring of the few-shot branch), needs no retraining, runs in hours on one GPU, and has measurable outcomes: AUROC change, sensitivity at fixed specificity, ECE, and the variance of an image's score when the rest of the test set is resampled.

Clarity.review: The three parts of the scoring pipeline that are replaced (test-set min-max, fixed 0.5 weight, max pooling) and the measurable criteria are precise. Bundling three changes makes it less clear which one drives any effect.
Clarity.feedback: Keep one problem but require an ablation order: normalisation first, then fusion weight, then aggregation.

Relevance.review: Directly addresses G8 (transductive normalisation verified in the code), G9 (max-pixel image score) and G11 (no thresholded metrics). Every published few-shot number of MVFA depends on the component in question.

Originality.review: Inductive score normalisation with validation statistics is standard practice in anomaly-detection tooling, and calibration of CLIP scores appears in CANOR. What is new is identifying that MVFA's reported results rely on transductive normalisation and measuring the deployment gap, including invariance to test-set composition.
Originality.feedback: Emphasise the invariance test (re-scoring an image under resampled test sets) as the novel measurement.

Feasibility.review: Inference-only: it reuses trained checkpoints and needs a few hours on one GPU.

Significance.review: Turns MVFA into a detector that can score one image at a time and reports thresholded clinical metrics; if AUROC drops, it also corrects the published comparison.
Significance.feedback: Report the per-image score shift as a headline number; it is what a deploying team needs.

versions.problem: How far do MVFA's published few-shot results depend on transductive test-set min-max normalisation, and can an inductive per-image score, in which each branch is standardised with statistics of the K normal support images and source-validation data, recover image AUROC within 1 point while making each image's score invariant to the rest of the test set? Changes are evaluated in a fixed order: normalisation first, then fusion weight, then image-level aggregation, with sensitivity at 95% specificity and expected calibration error reported alongside AUROC.
versions.rationale: The released code normalises each branch with the minimum and maximum over the entire test set before fusing with weight 0.5 (G8), takes the image label from the maximum of the fused map (G9), and reports only AUC (G11). A deployed detector scores one image at a time, so the published numbers are not those of a usable system, and the size of this gap has never been measured. Inductive normalisation with validation statistics is common in anomaly-detection tooling, and CANOR [55] calibrates CLIP scores with a handful of scalars, but no medical CLIP detector in the review set (LaRP-CLIP [17], HeadCLIP [4]) measures the effect of transductive normalisation on reported results. The headline measurement is new: the shift of an individual image's score when the rest of the test set is resampled (prevalence 10-50%, with and without outliers), for the original and the inductive pipeline. The ordered ablation attributes any change to one component at a time. The study is inference-only on retrained checkpoints and takes hours on one GPU.

Clarity.review: The ordered ablation and the invariance measurement make the study well defined. The statement is long and contains two questions (dependence on transductive normalisation and the inductive replacement).
Clarity.feedback: Lead with the single question (the inductive replacement) and present the dependence measurement as its baseline.

Relevance.review: Addresses G8, G9 and G11 directly, on the component every published few-shot number of MVFA depends on.

Originality.review: The invariance measurement is a new and useful diagnostic for medical CLIP detectors, but inductive normalisation and calibration are established techniques.
Originality.feedback: None needed; the measurement is the contribution.

Significance.review: Quantifies a deployment gap in a widely cited method and supplies thresholded metrics that clinical readers need.

versions.problem: Can MVFA's few-shot inference be made inductive, scoring each image only with statistics of the K normal support images and source-validation data instead of test-set min-max normalisation, while keeping image AUROC within 1 point of the re-run transductive baseline and making each image's score invariant to the composition of the rest of the test set (prevalence 10-50%, with and without outliers)? The replacement is evaluated component by component (normalisation, then fusion weight, then image-level aggregation), with sensitivity at 95% specificity and expected calibration error reported alongside AUROC.
versions.rationale: The released code min-max normalises each branch over the entire test set before fusing with weight 0.5 (G8), takes the image label from the maximum of the fused map (G9), and reports only AUC (G11). A deployed detector scores one image at a time, so the published numbers are not those of a usable system, and the size of the gap has not been measured. Inductive normalisation with validation statistics is common in anomaly-detection tooling and CANOR [55] calibrates CLIP scores with a few scalars, but no medical CLIP detector in the review set (LaRP-CLIP [17], HeadCLIP [4]) measures how transductive normalisation affects reported results. The headline measurement, the shift of an individual image's score when the rest of the test set is resampled, is a new diagnostic for this family of methods, and the transductive baseline's own shift is its reference. The study is inference-only on retrained checkpoints and takes hours on one GPU.

Clarity.review: The lead question is now clear, and the component-wise evaluation is specified. The statement remains long and carries several metrics and resampling settings in one sentence.
Clarity.feedback: Move the resampling settings into the rationale to keep the problem statement short.

Relevance.review: Addresses G8, G9 and G11 directly, on the scoring component behind all published few-shot results.

Originality.review: The score-invariance diagnostic is new for medical CLIP detectors; inductive normalisation itself is established.

Significance.review: Quantifies the deployment gap of a widely cited method and adds clinically interpretable metrics.

versions.problem: In MVFA's few-shot setting, can the K labelled abnormal support images with pixel masks be dropped entirely, adapting the residual adapters per target modality from the K normal support images alone with synthesised lesions (patch pasting and intensity-perturbed blobs whose synthetic masks supervise the Dice + Focal losses), and how much of the image- and pixel-level AUROC of the standard K-normal + K-masked-abnormal protocol does this normal-only variant retain for K in {2, 4, 8, 16}?
versions.rationale: The released code defines 'K-shot' as K normal plus K abnormal images with masks from BMAD's valid split (G4), so the paper's few-shot numbers assume the expensive part of clinical labelling, while a clinic adopting a new modality usually has only normal studies at hand; the segmentation branch has no other supervision route (G3). The review set shows that normal-only adaptation of CLIP is viable in other frameworks: MediCLIP [10] fine-tunes CLIP with medical anomaly synthesis from few normal images, SpatioPrompt [20] studies the normal-only few-shot setting explicitly, Fed-LoRA [56] and the UWF-fundus adapter [15] synthesise abnormal exemplars, and AnomalyUWF reports strong results from only 32 training pairs. None of these measures what MVFA's multi-level adapters lose when the abnormal support set is removed. The problem changes one input of one stage (the support set of the few-shot fine-tuning), needs only the public code and BMAD, and has a direct measurable outcome: the fraction of K+K performance retained per modality and K, with 3 support draws under the shared protocol.

Clarity.review: Clear setting (few-shot, K in 2-16), clear change (drop abnormal masked supports, add synthesised lesions) and clear outcome (fraction of K+K AUROC retained). The synthesis recipe is described only loosely.
Clarity.feedback: Fix the synthesis families and their parameters in the problem, or state that they follow MediCLIP's published recipe.

Relevance.review: Targets G4 directly: the few-shot protocol's hidden reliance on masked abnormal images is the main gap between MVFA's claims and clinical few-shot reality.
Relevance.feedback: Mention that the same 3-draw protocol answers the single-draw part of G4.

Originality.review: Normal-only few-shot adaptation of CLIP with anomaly synthesis is exactly what MediCLIP and SpatioPrompt study; the problem transfers their setting to MVFA's adapters. The contribution is an ablation of MVFA's protocol rather than a new challenge.
Originality.feedback: Add a distinctive angle, for example whether synthetic supervision should be applied only to the segmentation branch or to both branches, or how synthesis interacts with MVFA's zero-shot pre-training.

Feasibility.review: Few-shot fine-tuning on K images is minutes per run; synthesis is cheap; all comparisons use public code and data.
Feasibility.feedback: None beyond fixing the synthesis recipe.

Significance.review: Quantifying the retained performance is practically useful, but the expected result (synthesis recovers part of the gap) is predictable from MediCLIP and SpatioPrompt.
Significance.feedback: Explain what decision the result would change, e.g. whether clinics need any annotated abnormal studies at all.

versions.problem: When MVFA's few-shot adaptation receives only K normal support images (no abnormal images, no masks), should synthesised lesions supervise only the segmentation adapters, only the detection adapters, or both, and how much of the image- and pixel-level AUROC of the standard K-normal + K-masked-abnormal protocol does the best normal-only variant retain for K in {2, 4, 8, 16} over three support draws?
versions.rationale: The released code defines 'K-shot' as K normal plus K abnormal images with masks (G4), so MVFA's few-shot numbers assume the expensive part of clinical labelling, and the segmentation branch has no other route to supervision (G3). MediCLIP [10] and SpatioPrompt [20] show that CLIP can be adapted from normal images with anomaly synthesis, but in single-branch designs; MVFA separates detection and segmentation adapters at four levels, and synthetic lesions are known to transfer imperfectly to real pathology, so which branch should consume synthetic supervision is an open design question specific to the target method. Synthesis follows MediCLIP's published recipe (fixed families and parameters), so the only variable is where the synthetic supervision is applied. The outcome answers a practical question, whether a clinic needs any annotated abnormal studies to adapt MVFA, and the three-draw protocol also answers the single-draw part of G4. Few-shot fine-tuning takes minutes per run on one GPU.

Clarity.review: The branch question and the fixed synthesis recipe make the problem well defined; the outcome is clear. The problem statement still mixes two questions (which branch, how much retained).
Clarity.feedback: Make the retained fraction the outcome of the branch comparison rather than a second question.

Relevance.review: Directly addresses G4, including the single-draw issue, and the lack of a normal-only route in G3.

Originality.review: Asking which of MVFA's two branches should consume synthetic supervision is specific to the target method and not answered by MediCLIP or SpatioPrompt; the underlying normal-only setting is still known.

Significance.review: Practical, but the likely answer (both branches, partial recovery) has limited impact beyond MVFA.
Significance.feedback: Report the minimal K at which normal-only matches K+K, which is the actionable number.

versions.problem: When MVFA is adapted from K normal support images only, with synthesised lesions following MediCLIP's recipe, does applying the synthetic supervision to the segmentation adapters, the detection adapters, or both retain the most of the image- and pixel-level AUROC of the standard K-normal + K-masked-abnormal protocol, and what is the smallest K at which the best normal-only variant matches the K+K protocol (K in {2, 4, 8, 16}, three support draws)?
versions.rationale: The released code defines 'K-shot' as K normal plus K abnormal images with masks (G4), so MVFA's few-shot results assume abnormal annotations that a clinic adopting a new modality rarely has, and the segmentation branch has no other route to supervision (G3). MediCLIP [10] and SpatioPrompt [20] show normal-only adaptation of CLIP with synthetic anomalies in single-branch designs; MVFA's separate detection and segmentation adapters raise a question those papers do not answer: which branch benefits from synthetic supervision, given that synthetic lesions transfer imperfectly to real pathology. The synthesis recipe is fixed, so the branch choice is the only variable. The smallest K at which normal-only adaptation matches K+K is the actionable number for deployment, and three support draws also answer the single-draw part of G4. Each few-shot run takes minutes on one GPU.

Clarity.review: A single comparison (which branch receives synthetic supervision) with a fixed recipe and an actionable outcome (smallest K matching K+K).

Relevance.review: Directly addresses G4, including the single-draw issue, and the absence of a normal-only route in G3.

Originality.review: The branch question is specific to MVFA's two-branch design; the normal-only synthetic setting is established.

Feasibility.review: Minutes per run; public code and data.

Significance.review: Actionable for MVFA users, but the impact on the wider field is limited because the setting is already studied in single-branch methods.

versions.problem: Does replacing MVFA's frozen, hand-crafted normal/abnormal prompts (state words averaged over 35 ImageNet templates) with a small set of learnable prompt tokens conditioned on the image's adapted patch features improve zero-shot pixel- and image-level AUROC on a held-out BMAD modality, and does it reduce the sensitivity of MVFA's results to the choice of prompt wording?
versions.rationale: MVFA assumes one universal text notion of 'normal' and 'abnormal' across modalities and never analyses prompt sensitivity (G5), although the relation between a compact normal concept and diverse abnormal ones is central to anomaly detection (G7). Most recent CLIP detectors in the review set replace static prompts: AnomalyCLIP [11] learns object-agnostic prompts, AdaCLIP [32] combines static and image-specific dynamic prompts, CoPS [41] and VCF-CLIP [22] synthesise prompts from visual prototypes, IQE-CLIP [7] builds instance-aware query embeddings, and prompt-wording studies on medical vision-language models report unstable performance [50]. Their effect has not been isolated inside MVFA's multi-level adapter framework, where prompts interact with every level's alignment loss. The question changes one component (the text side of the alignment) while keeping the visual adapters fixed in design, is trainable on one GPU, and has measurable outcomes: AUROC on held-out modalities and the spread of AUROC across a fixed set of alternative prompt wordings.

Clarity.review: Clear change (learnable, visually conditioned prompt tokens), clear setting (zero-shot, held-out modality) and two outcomes including prompt-wording sensitivity.
Clarity.feedback: Define the conditioning mechanism and the size of the token set, and the fixed list of alternative wordings.

Relevance.review: Addresses G5 directly and G7 only loosely.
Relevance.feedback: Drop the G7 claim or explain how conditioned prompts model the normal/abnormal asymmetry.

Originality.review: Learnable and visually conditioned prompts are the dominant design in the review set (AnomalyCLIP, AdaCLIP, CoPS, VCF-CLIP, IQE-CLIP). Inserting one into MVFA is an incremental combination.
Originality.feedback: Focus on an under-studied aspect, e.g. whether learned prompts transfer across modalities in the leave-one-modality-out split, which none of these papers isolates.

Feasibility.review: Requires training text tokens jointly with adapters; feasible on one GPU but adds hyper-parameters.
Feasibility.feedback: Freeze the visual adapters from MVFA's checkpoint and train only prompts to keep cost low.

Significance.review: Expected gains are modest because MVFA's adapters already align features with fixed prompts.
Significance.feedback: Report the sensitivity reduction as the main outcome; it is the part not covered by prior work.

versions.problem: Do prompts learned on source modalities transfer to an unseen modality inside MVFA? With MVFA's visual adapters frozen at their trained checkpoint, learnable normal/abnormal prompt tokens (16 tokens per state, optionally conditioned on the mean adapted patch feature) are trained on the source modalities and compared with the fixed 35-template prompts on the held-out modality, measuring zero-shot AUROC and the spread of AUROC across ten alternative prompt wordings.
versions.rationale: MVFA assumes a single universal text notion of normal and abnormal across modalities and never analyses prompt sensitivity (G5). Learnable and visually conditioned prompts are common in the review set (AnomalyCLIP [11], AdaCLIP [32], CoPS [41], VCF-CLIP [22], IQE-CLIP [7]), and medical prompt studies report unstable performance across wordings [50], but none isolates cross-modality transfer of learned prompts under a modality-disjoint split, which is the setting MVFA claims. Freezing the visual adapters isolates the text side and keeps training cheap. The main outcome is the reduction in wording sensitivity; the AUROC change on held-out modalities is secondary.

Clarity.review: Clear set-up with frozen adapters, fixed token count and a fixed set of wordings.
Clarity.feedback: Specify how the ten wordings are chosen (e.g. clinical vs generic).

Relevance.review: Addresses G5; G7 is no longer claimed, which is appropriate.

Originality.review: Cross-modality transfer of learned prompts under a modality-disjoint split is not isolated in the review set, although learned prompts themselves are common.

Feasibility.review: Training only prompt tokens on frozen adapters is cheap.

Significance.review: Sensitivity reduction is useful, but the impact is limited to the text side of one method.

Clarity.review: Frozen adapters, fixed token count, conditioning option and a fixed set of ten wordings make the study precise.

Originality.review: Cross-modality transfer of learned prompts under a modality-disjoint split is not isolated in prior work, though learned prompts are common.

Significance.review: Limited to the text side of one method; useful mainly as a robustness finding.

versions.problem: Can MVFA's few-shot patch memory bank, which stores every adapted patch feature of the K normal support images at four levels, be replaced by a compact parametric model of normal patch features per level (a small set of prototypes or a Gaussian with shrinkage covariance), and how does this change few-shot pixel- and image-level AUROC, memory footprint and per-image inference time as K grows from 2 to 16?
versions.rationale: MVFA compares query patches with a memory bank whose size grows linearly with K and with spatial resolution, without modelling the compact distribution of normal tissue against the diverse distribution of anomalies (G7), and its retrieval cost and the privacy implication of storing raw patient-derived features are not analysed (G13). Related work points toward explicit compact normality: AVA-DINO [14] exploits the asymmetry of compact normals versus diverse anomalies, Spatial-FAD [6] stores compact normal and abnormal prototypes to cut memory while improving few-shot localisation, and the Consistency Margin Adapter [21] aligns representations with a normal reference through margin objectives. Whether a compact normal model suffices for MVFA's adapted features has not been tested. The question isolates one component (the few-shot comparison against stored normals), is feasible because it needs no retraining of the adapters, and has measurable outcomes: AUROC differences relative to the full bank, bytes stored per support image, latency, and the K at which the compact model matches the bank.

Clarity.review: Clear component (few-shot memory bank), two named replacements, clear outcomes including memory and latency as functions of K.
Clarity.feedback: Specify how prototypes are obtained (k-means per level, number of prototypes) so the comparison is reproducible.

Relevance.review: Addresses G13 (memory, retrieval cost, storage of patient features) and part of G7 (explicit compact normal model); G5 is not touched.
Relevance.feedback: State the privacy benefit precisely: a parametric model stores statistics rather than raw patch features.

Originality.review: Gaussian normal models (PaDiM) and compact prototypes (Spatial-FAD) are known; applying them to MVFA's adapted multi-level features with a K-scaling analysis adds a moderate new angle.
Originality.feedback: Add the question of whether the adapted features are more Gaussian than raw CLIP features, which would explain when compact models suffice.

Feasibility.review: No retraining; fitting a Gaussian or k-means on support features is seconds.

Significance.review: Useful for deployment cost and privacy, but the bank is small at K <= 16, so practical gains may be limited.
Significance.feedback: Include a high-resolution or larger-K setting where the bank's cost actually matters.

versions.problem: Are MVFA's adapted patch features compact enough that a per-level Gaussian with shrinkage covariance, or 32 k-means prototypes, fitted on the K normal support images can replace the few-shot memory bank of raw patch features without losing more than 1 point of pixel or image AUROC, and how do memory, latency and the information stored about patients scale with K (2-64) and input resolution (240 and 448) for each option?
versions.rationale: MVFA compares query patches with a memory bank that grows linearly with K and resolution, stores raw patient-derived features, and never models the compact distribution of normal tissue explicitly (G7, G13). Gaussian normal models (PaDiM) and compact prototypes (Spatial-FAD [6]) work for other features, and AVA-DINO [14] argues that normals are compact and anomalies diverse; whether MVFA's adapted features have this property has not been measured. The study first tests Gaussianity of adapted versus raw CLIP features per level, which explains when a compact model suffices, then compares the three options in a regime where the bank's cost matters (K up to 64, 448-pixel input). A parametric model stores statistics rather than raw features, which is the privacy benefit G13 asks about. No retraining is needed; each fit takes seconds.

Clarity.review: Clear options, thresholds and scaling axes; the Gaussianity test is well motivated.
Clarity.feedback: Name the Gaussianity test (e.g. Mardia's or a per-dimension check) to keep it reproducible.

Relevance.review: Addresses G13 and the compactness part of G7.

Originality.review: Testing whether adapted features are more Gaussian than raw CLIP features is a new diagnostic; the compact models themselves are known.

Significance.review: K = 64 and 448-pixel inputs are outside MVFA's protocol, so the practical relevance of the cost gains is limited.
Significance.feedback: Justify the extended regime with a clinical scenario.

versions.problem: Are MVFA's adapted patch features compact enough that a per-level Gaussian with shrinkage covariance, or 32 k-means prototypes, fitted on the K normal support images can replace the few-shot memory bank without losing more than 1 point of pixel or image AUROC, and how do memory, latency and stored patient information scale with K (2-64) and input resolution (240 and 448) for each option, in a scenario where a site accumulates normal studies over time?
versions.rationale: MVFA compares query patches with a memory bank that grows with K and resolution and stores raw patient-derived features (G13), without modelling the compact normal distribution explicitly (G7). PaDiM-style Gaussians and Spatial-FAD's compact prototypes [6] work for other features, and AVA-DINO [14] argues normals are compact while anomalies are diverse; whether MVFA's adapted features share this property is untested. The study first tests per-level Gaussianity of adapted versus raw CLIP features (Mardia's multivariate skewness and kurtosis on a random projection), then compares the three options. The extended K and resolution model a site that keeps adding normal studies, where a growing raw-feature bank becomes a storage and governance burden. No retraining is needed.

Clarity.review: Clear options, test and scaling axes; the 'stored patient information' outcome is not operationalised.
Clarity.feedback: Define it, e.g. as bytes stored per patient or feasibility of reconstructing patches from stored statistics.

Relevance.review: Addresses G13 and the compactness aspect of G7.

Originality.review: The Gaussianity diagnostic on adapted features is new; compact normal models are known.

Significance.review: Mostly relevant to long-term deployment scenarios outside MVFA's few-shot protocol.

versions.problem: Which image-level pooling of MVFA's anomaly maps (max as in the paper's Eq. 3, mean as in the released training code, top-k mean, or a noisy-OR over patches), applied consistently in training and testing, gives the best and most robust image-level detection, measured by image AUROC and by its degradation when a small fraction of spurious high-scoring pixels is injected into normal test maps?
versions.rationale: The paper defines the image-level loss with a max over the anomaly map, while the released code mean-pools in training and takes the max of the fused segmentation map at test time on masked datasets (G17, G9), so a single spurious pixel can decide an image's label and the reported results cannot be attributed to the method as described. No robust aggregation is tested, and AUC alone hides how fragile the score is (G11). The related work treats the map-to-image step as a design choice: CANOR [55] replaces naive max/mean aggregation with a calibrated noisy-OR, HeadCLIP [4] builds a joint score from pixel-level evidence, and LaRP-CLIP [17] adds a prototype branch because image scores from global similarity are unreliable. The question is narrow (one pooling operator, used consistently), cheap (the pooling changes one line in training and one in testing, so each variant is a single retraining), and measurable on BMAD: image AUROC per held-out modality, and the drop in AUROC under controlled spurious-pixel injection.

Clarity.review: One operator, applied consistently in training and testing, four named variants, two named metrics including a controlled spurious-pixel stress test.

Relevance.review: Addresses G17 and G9 directly; G11 only through the robustness test.
Relevance.feedback: Tie the stress test to a clinical artefact (e.g. bright vessels or acquisition noise) to strengthen relevance.

Originality.review: Choosing among max, mean, top-k and noisy-OR is a standard ablation; CANOR already proposes noisy-OR aggregation for CLIP chest X-ray scores. The paper/code mismatch is a reproducibility finding rather than a research challenge.
Originality.feedback: Frame a hypothesis about why one pooling suits MVFA (e.g. lesion size distribution per modality) to go beyond a sweep.

Feasibility.review: One-line changes in training and testing; four retrainings.

Significance.review: Resolves an attribution question for MVFA and gives a robustness number, but the likely effect sizes are modest.
Significance.feedback: Report results stratified by lesion size, where the choice should matter most.

versions.problem: Does the best image-level pooling of MVFA's anomaly maps depend on lesion size? Comparing max (paper, Eq. 3), mean (released training code), top-k mean with k tied to the source datasets' median lesion area, and noisy-OR, each applied identically in training and testing, which gives the highest image AUROC per held-out modality, and how does each degrade when spurious high-scoring pixels mimicking bright vessels or acquisition noise are injected into normal test maps?
versions.rationale: The paper and the released code disagree on pooling (G17), and the test-time image score on masked datasets is the maximum of the fused map, so one spurious pixel can decide the label (G9); robustness is never measured (G11). CANOR [55] shows that noisy-OR beats naive max/mean aggregation for CLIP chest X-ray scores, and LaRP-CLIP [17] and HeadCLIP [4] build image scores from pixel evidence, but none relates the choice to lesion size, which differs by an order of magnitude across BMAD (small brain lesions, larger liver tumours, diffuse retinal fluid). The hypothesis is that max suits small lesions and top-k or noisy-OR suit large or diffuse ones. Each variant is a one-line change in training and testing, so four retrainings suffice; results are stratified by lesion-size tertiles on the masked datasets.

Clarity.review: Clear variants and hypothesis; the k-to-lesion-area rule needs a definition for datasets without masks.
Clarity.feedback: State how k is set for the image-only datasets (e.g. median over the masked sources).

Relevance.review: Addresses G17 and G9; G11 through the robustness test.

Originality.review: Relating the pooling choice to lesion size across modalities gives a testable hypothesis beyond a sweep.

Significance.review: Useful for attribution and robustness, with modest expected effect sizes.

versions.problem: Does the best image-level pooling of MVFA's anomaly maps depend on lesion size? Comparing max (paper, Eq. 3), mean (released training code), top-k mean with k set to the median lesion area of the masked source datasets, and noisy-OR, each applied identically in training and testing, which gives the highest image AUROC per held-out modality and per lesion-size tertile, and how does each degrade when spurious high-scoring pixels mimicking bright vessels or acquisition noise are injected into normal test maps?
versions.rationale: The paper and the released code disagree on pooling (G17), and the test-time image score on masked datasets is the maximum of the fused map, so a single spurious pixel can decide the label (G9); robustness is not measured (G11). CANOR [55] shows that noisy-OR improves on naive max/mean aggregation for CLIP chest X-ray scores, and LaRP-CLIP [17] and HeadCLIP [4] build image scores from pixel evidence, but none relates the choice to lesion size, which varies by an order of magnitude across BMAD. The hypothesis is that max suits small focal lesions and top-k or noisy-OR suit large or diffuse ones; k is fixed from the masked sources and reused for the image-only datasets. Each variant is a one-line change in training and testing, so four retrainings suffice.

Clarity.review: Clear variants, hypothesis and stratification; the injection of spurious pixels needs a quantitative specification (number, intensity).

Originality.review: The lesion-size hypothesis turns a sweep into a testable question.

Significance.review: Resolves a paper/code discrepancy and informs pooling choices, with modest expected effects.
